segments.caption: A model can score well on its own and still not change what clinicians do.
segments.text: A benchmark asks whether the model can answer. A trial asks whether clinicians do better with it. These are different questions, and only the second one decides whether a tool helps patients.

segments.caption: Goh et al. randomized 50 physicians into two groups of 25.
segments.text: Goh and colleagues randomized fifty physicians: twenty-five to G P T four plus their usual resources, and twenty-five to usual resources alone. Both groups worked up to six vignettes in sixty minutes, graded blind on a structured reflection rubric.

segments.caption: Median score per case: 76% with GPT-4, 74% without.
segments.text: The median diagnostic reasoning score per case was seventy-six percent with G P T four and seventy-four percent without. The adjusted difference was two percentage points, with a ninety-five percent interval from minus four to eight and a P value of zero point six zero. The interval includes zero.

segments.caption: Nor was it faster: 519 seconds per case against 565.
segments.text: Nor was it faster. Physicians with the model took five hundred nineteen seconds per case against five hundred sixty-five, a difference of minus eighty-two seconds, with a ninety-five percent interval from minus one hundred ninety-five to thirty-one. That interval includes zero too.

segments.caption: GPT-4 alone scored 92%, 16 points above the control group.
segments.text: In an exploratory arm of three runs, the model alone scored a median of ninety-two percent, sixteen points above the control group. But the physicians who had that same model scored seventy-six. The gap is about how people use the tool, not about the tool.

segments.caption: Each rung of the evaluation ladder answers a question the one below cannot.
segments.text: Benchmark, retrospective study, reader study, prospective trial, then deployment with monitoring. Each rung answers a question the one below it cannot. This trial is the fourth rung, and most published results stop at the first.
